title: Cayley–Hamilton theorem
section: The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem ▷ Reducing Matrix Powers
terms: Cayley-Hamilton theorem; characteristic identity; reduction of matrix powers.

exposition.text:
Cayley–Hamilton states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial:
n n−1
χ (A) = 0. If χ (t) = t + c t + · · · + c , substitute A for t and c I for the constant term.
A A n−1 0 0
Consequently every nonnegative power of A can be expressed as a polynomial of degree less
than n in A.

For a two-by-two matrix this gives A − (tr A)A + (det A)I = 0, so all powers reduce to combina-
tions of I, A. For larger matrices the reduction is not necessarily linear in A. Divide the desired
scalar polynomial by χ and evaluate the remainder at A; this often avoids direct multiplica-

An annihilating polynomial p satisfies p(A) = 0 but need not have the same degree or multiplici-

question.text:
2
A real 2 × 2 matrix has characteristic polynomial (t − 1) . Without assuming diagonalizability,
which formula is guaranteed?
100 100
(A) A = I (B) A = 100A
100 100
(C) A = 100A − 99I (D) A = 99A − 100I
100 99
(E) A = 2 A

solution.text:
2 2
Cayley–Hamilton gives (A − I) = 0. Write A = I + N with N = 0; the binomial expansion
100
terminates at A = I + 100N = 100A − 99I. Knowing only the repeated eigenvalue does
not justify replacing A by I.

question.text:
For A = diag(−1, 0, 1), which assertion is true?
2
(A) A = aA + bI for some real a, b.
3 2
(B) A = A, but A is not a linear combination of I and A.
2
(C) A = I.
(D) A is invertible.
(E) A does not satisfy its characteristic polynomial.

solution.text:
3 3 2
The characteristic polynomial is t(t − 1)(t + 1) = t − t, so A = A. If A = aA + bI, the zero
diagonal position forces b = 0; the positions for eigenvalues 1 and −1 then force a = 1 and
a = −1, a contradiction. In size three a quadratic remainder can be necessary.

question.text:
2
A real 3 × 3 matrix satisfies A − 3A + 2I = 0. Which polynomial could be its characteristic
polynomial?
2
(A) t − 3t + 2 (B) (t − 1)(t − 2)(t − 3)
2 3
(C) (t − 1) (t − 2) (D) t − 1
2
(E) (t − 1) (t + 2)

solution.text:
2
Every eigenvalue must be a root of t − 3t + 2, hence must be 1 or 2, while a three-by-three
characteristic polynomial has degree three. Only C satisfies both requirements, and it is
realized by diag(1, 1, 2). An annihilating polynomial need not itself be the characteristic
polynomial.

question.text:
3 −1
A matrix A has characteristic polynomial t − t − 1. Which expression is (A − I) ?
2 2 2 2
(A) A − I (B) A + A (C) A − A (D) I − A (E) A + I

solution.text:
3 2
Cayley–Hamilton gives A − A = I. Factoring the left side as (A − I)(A + A) proves the
stated inverse; the factors commute because they are polynomials in A. This also proves
invertibility of the shifted matrix directly.

question.text:
3
A real 3 × 3 matrix has characteristic polynomial t . Which assertion must hold?
2 3
(A) A = 0 (B) A = 0 (C) A = 0 (D) rank A = 1 (E) dim ker A = 2

solution.text:
3
Cayley–Hamilton gives A = 0. The matrix with ones immediately above the diagonal and
zeros elsewhere has rank two, a one-dimensional kernel, and a nonzero square, so none of
the stronger claims is necessary.
